extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, parties and counsel involved in USPTO Board contested cases and patent interference proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, definitions, and content/timing requirements governing motions, oppositions, discovery, evidence, counts, priority proofs, and other practice in USPTO contested cases and patent interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation/disclaimer of claims and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorization to cancel a claim under § 41.121(a)(2) is removed as an express option to avoid casual requests; a patentee can disclaim a claim under 35 U.S.C. 253, but cancellation/disclaimer can have consequences including judgment against the canceling party and estoppel under § 41.127(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cancellation does not mean consequence-free: cancellation of all involved claims can result in judgment against the canceling party (§ 41.127(b)(2)); cancellation in response to an attack concedes the issue for that claim and creates estoppel similar to amending a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standards are issue-specific (no blanket preponderance codification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all motions are subject to a preponderance standard; some issues (e.g., priority for a junior party who filed after a senior party's patent) require clear and convincing evidence (§ 41.207(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codifying preponderance as a default would require listing every exception; leaving standards as currently applied avoids confusion—default civil standard is preponderance but exceptions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions must substantively prove their case (content over checklist compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.121(c) sets general requirements; compliance with a detailed technical checklist like § 1.637 (2003) did not guarantee survival because movants must still carry the substantive burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movants cannot rely on form alone to avoid dismissal; the Board may develop practice notes, but substance remains decisive (see Hillman, 55 USPQ2d at 1221).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of material facts: single-sentence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Material facts must be stated to permit the opposing party readily to admit or deny them; multi-sentence or long compound sentences are abusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: § 41.121(d)(1) adds a single-sentence requirement for each material fact to avoid parsing difficulties and facilitate decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of burden when adding a claim — proving patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Obligation to 'prove patentability' when adding a claim is generally limited to showing compliance with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(1), except where the party reasonably has actual notice of other patentability problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual notice typically comes from prior rejections in the prosecution history or a substantive motion by the opposing party; opponents should explain issues in opposition rather than merely pointing them out; movants should explain lack of notice in their reply if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed explanation of significance of evidence required
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing a numbered material fact or a portion of an exhibit is permitted but is not a substitute for explaining what the evidence means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments must provide context and meaning; mere citation recruits the Board and opposing party to make the case—burden to explain how evidence justifies relief remains with filing party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of 37 CFR part 1 rules to contested-case relief
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.121(c)(2) requires compliance with any Part 1 rule that would govern the relief sought if sought outside a contested case, but practical complications exist (e.g., movant might not be the reissue applicant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules cannot foresee every contingency; harms from inadequate filings (e.g., reissue declarations) can be addressed in opposition or via a miscellaneous motion (§ 41.121(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material facts not denied are deemed admitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Any material fact not denied will be considered admitted; placing the fact in a paper already places it in issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring that a fact be 'placed in issue' before it can be deemed admitted would lead to fruitless disputes about 'placement'; the Board invites notice of abuses where statements obtain extraneous admissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses to material facts should be admit or deny (no 'not admitted')
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting a 'not admitted' response to facts not supported by exhibits was not adopted; a denial alone is preferred; silence results in admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Not admitted' responses are not helpful: if party agrees despite exhibit inadequacy, admit; otherwise deny and, if useful, alert opposing party to the defect so it can be corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim charts: form and page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim charts help illustrate a claim's meaning in comparison to prior art, other claims, or a specification; no specific form is required and the rules set no page limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each party has incentive to produce clear claim charts; absence of a mandated form allows flexibility and tailoring to the point to be illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on new arguments in oppositions and replies
rubrics_metrics.description: Second sentence of proposed § 41.122 (confusing) deleted; arguments first made in a reply are not attributed to the motion and thus do not cure the motion's deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply cannot be used to cure defects first noted in an opposition; scope of opposition argument clarified to avoid improper expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default right to file oppositions and replies but subject to Board control
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing oppositions and replies is the default in contested cases, but the Board has authority to set times and determine when such filings are authorized (oppositions not automatic for miscellaneous motions per § 41.123(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The default reflects common practice; Board may authorize or deny oppositions/replies when filings would be moot or otherwise inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default times for filing (tailorable by Board)
rubrics_metrics.description: Default times in § 41.123(a) and (b)(2) are defaults to be used if no times set by order; the Board official administering the case will typically tailor times appropriate to each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsive motions typically filed before oppositions; parties can suggest different times when motions are authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default times for miscellaneous motions and authorization requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Default times for miscellaneous motions in § 41.123(b)(2) mirror Standing Order ¶ 13.10.2; opposed miscellaneous motions must be authorized (§ 41.123(b)(1)(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a motion is authorized, parties can propose different opposition/reply times in the authorization order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit filing and service with first paper citing them
rubrics_metrics.description: Default rule (§ 41.123(c)) requires that an exhibit be filed and served with the first paper citing it; previously filed or served exhibits need not be refiled or re-served.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current practice often defers filing exhibits until shortly before motions will be decided; see § 41.7(b) regarding duplicate filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral argument time default and requesting additional time
rubrics_metrics.description: Default total time for oral argument for each party is twenty minutes regardless of number of issues (§ 41.124(c)); the Board may authorize different amounts (§ 41.104(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active bench questioning may result in more time in practice; parties needing more time should file a miscellaneous motion (§ 41.121(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcript and filed papers become part of the record if properly filed
rubrics_metrics.description: Any paper properly filed (including oral argument transcripts) becomes part of the record; improperly filed papers may be expunged (§ 41.7(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a transcript does not require special wording—proper filing suffices; parties may seek expungement for improper filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of addressing motions is discretionary with Board
rubrics_metrics.description: Board ultimately decides the order of consideration, though parties may mark papers as contingent or discuss order during conferences; threshold issues may be advanced while others deferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can express opinions about order (contingent markings, conference discussions), but must keep in mind Board discretion; common practice defers certain issues like priority-phase matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness standard is 'no abuse of discretion'
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring the Board's order to be 'reasonable' is superfluous—Board discretionary actions are subject to review for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Reasonable' in this context simply indicates that discretionary action must not be an abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing request must point to prior filings or show issue was not raised
rubrics_metrics.description: A rehearing request must point to where the matter was previously addressed in a motion, opposition, or reply (§ 41.125(c)(3)(ii)); if the Board reached an issue sua sponte, pointing out it was not previously addressed complies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when issue was not raised earlier, the rehearing must identify what the Board misapprehended or overlooked (§ 41.125(c)(3)(i)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel from adverse judgment on patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that loses on patentability for an involved claim receives an adverse judgment and is estopped with respect to patentability of that claim's subject matter (§ 41.127(a)); priority is effectively a question of unpatentability under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One never 'prevails' on priority in an absolute sense—priority determinations are framed as losses on the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listed grounds for adverse judgment (abandonment/disclaimer omitted as redundant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment or disclaimer of the invention of the count (grounds under § 1.662 (2003)) were omitted from § 41.127(b) as redundant with other grounds, with no practical effect other than brevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission was for brevity and does not change substantive outcome where covered by other grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely request for reconsideration tolls judicial review period
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolling the time for seeking judicial review is automatic with a timely request for reconsideration; the decision on rehearing is itself a final decision for purposes of judicial review timing (In re Graves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The previous sentence regarding discretionary tolling was removed as unnecessary under case law; reconsideration resets the judicial review timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and effect of termination during judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Termination of an interference proceeding for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 135(c) is defined in § 41.205(a) (incorporating and modifying former Rule 661); issuance of the appellate court's mandate controls termination unless stayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties settling during judicial review should note the effect of termination rules and that proceedings are considered terminated with issuance of the mandate absent a stay (Rule 197(b)(2) and 41.205(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for misleading or frivolous arguments and dilatory tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.128(a) provides for sanctions for misleading arguments (distinct from frivolous), frivolous arguments, and dilatory tactics; 'misleading' requires judgment but is no more subjective than 'frivolous'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions guard against abuse; dilatory tactics may be sanctionable even if delay was initially granted in good faith and later abused; inclusion emphasizes Board's commitment to avoiding undue delay (patent term adjustments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic service list includes applications incorporated by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.150(b)(1)(i) was modified to add patent applications incorporated by reference into an involved patent or application to the list of materials that must be automatically served upon request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted change to ensure relevant incorporated material is available to requesting parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional discovery must be authorized and guarded against fishing expeditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for additional discovery under § 41.150(c) must be authorized (usually by miscellaneous motion § 41.121(a)(3)); authorization historically protects against fishing expeditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: § 41.150(c) divided to add paragraph restoring production of documents and things under § 1.687(b) (2003); movant may be required to show evidence is not available elsewhere and necessary to establish prima facie basis for relief in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of Federal Rules of Evidence and exceptions (foreign law)
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.152 addresses when and how the Federal Rules of Evidence are applied; determination of foreign law (moved from § 41.156(c) to § 41.152(d)) can be an exception to use of FRE and is relevant to §§ 41.156 and 41.157.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign law determination is treated as a potential exception to the FRE in contested-case evidentiary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default timing for objections to evidence (five business days)
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.155(b)(1) requires objections to be filed within five business days of service of evidence as a default; the period can be extended on request (§§ 41.104(c) and 41.121(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five-day period has been longstanding in Standing Order ¶ 14.1.1 with few problems; extensions are available when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection waiver rule preserved and motion-to-exclude requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing Order ¶ 14.1.2's rule that an objection not made on the record is deemed waived is preserved in § 41.155(c); a motion to exclude must point to where the objection was made in the record; objections first raised in a motion to exclude are untimely (§ 41.4(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely objections on the record are required to avoid waiver; motion to exclude must cite record location of earlier objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental evidence and limits on subsequent objections
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.155(b)(2) does not authorize a second objection to supplemental evidence; the objector should make all objections to the first evidence; supplemental evidence either cures or fails to cure initial objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If supplemental evidence fails to cure, the objecting party should pursue the initial objection with a motion to exclude explaining why supplementation did not cure the defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelled testimony (subpoena) distinct from other discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Compelled testimony involving issuance of a subpoena under 35 U.S.C. 24 (addressed in § 41.156) involves different considerations from other discovery under § 41.150.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different statutory authority and process apply to compelled testimony; rules distinguish subpoena-based compelled testimony from ordinary discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony outside the United States requires multiple considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.157(b)(2)(ii) does not allow party stipulation alone to guarantee authorization of foreign testimony; parties' agreement is only one of many factors the Board will consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorization of foreign testimony depends on multiple factors beyond mere stipulation, and the Board retains discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errata corrections must reflect original Q&A; material changes may be falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections to testimony (errata) that materially alter testimony may amount to falsification and expose the party or counsel to sanctions; requiring accuracy of corrections will not eliminate abuse but misuse can be sanctionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a correction substantively changes testimony, promptly bring issue to Board's attention; sanctions can follow for falsified corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of counts: plain language primary, claims/specs may inform
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.200(b) provides that the count defines the interfering subject matter and its primary meaning is based on the plain language of the count; corresponding claims and involved specifications can set bounds on what the count reasonably means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since § 41.200(b) permits reference to the specification in interpreting claims, specifications can indirectly influence the broadest reasonable construction of the count via the claim defining the count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'accorded benefit' tied to constructive reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.201's definition of 'accorded benefit' is limited to what would constitute a constructive reduction to practice under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1), taking into account related statutes and case law; focus is on priority proofs rather than benefit under § 120.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule aims to avoid conflating 'benefit' in § 120 sense with interference priority concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reduction to practice definition and continuity (co-dependency) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of 'constructive reduction to practice' is tied to anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1); it can be satisfied by disclosure and enablement of the full scope of the count or by disclosure/enablement of something within the scope, and continuity/co-dependency in chain of applications is required for earliest constructive reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition revised to reflect anticipation principles; continuity requirement made clear by relocating 'earliest constructive reduction to practice' definition into revised definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentably distinct test for separate counts (one-way test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two counts must be 'patentably distinct'—a term of art meaning a difference such that one count, treated as prior art, would neither anticipate nor render obvious the subject matter of the other; a one-way test is sufficient to justify separate counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase derives from case law (Hester, Aelony); two-way distinctness is more than required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold issues: 35 U.S.C. 135(b) bar and written description
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 135(b) bar and written description issues are designated as threshold issues, particularly narrowed to provoked interferences to address perceived abuses (e.g., copying claims to provoke interferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description as a threshold issue prevents applicants from provoking interferences to obtain inter partes challenges; the threshold list is inclusive, and other issues (e.g., enablement) may be treated as threshold in future adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for suggesting an interference — propose at least one count
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.202(a)(2) was modified to require an applicant suggesting an interference to propose at least one count and explain correspondence to the count (§ 41.202(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation of correspondence to the count is required; a suggestion without a proposed count is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying interfering claims and using published-application claims at decision time
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant suggesting an interference must identify the claims that interfere and explain how they correspond to the suggested count; in the case of a published application, the decision is based on claims pending in the published application at the time of decision; no interference declared until both applications have allowable claims that still interfere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relevant claims for published applications may differ from those published; interference declaration awaits allowable interfering claims in both applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation vs actual showing of priority depending on filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.202(a)(4) requires an applicant suggesting an interference to provide a detailed explanation of why it will prevail on priority; § 41.202(d) requires an actual showing of priority when the applicant does not have the earlier effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant has the earliest effective filing date, explanation should be straightforward; where earlier filing date lacking, a more thorough showing is required so no interference is necessary on the face of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing supporting disclosure or constructive reduction to practice for interfering subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: § 41.202(a)(6)'s chart requirement was modified to require demonstration of a constructive reduction to practice within the scope of the interfering subject matter (rather than only a specific embodiment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'constructive reduction to practice' is tied to anticipation under § 102(g)(1), showing may consist of disclosure/enablement of the full scope or something within the scope of the interfering subject matter.
